title: An end-to-end quantum algorithm for weakly nonlinear plasma physics with superquadratic speedup
authors: Bjorn K. Berntson, David Jennings, Matteo Lostaglio, Scott Parker
abstract: Nonlinear kinetic plasma simulation is high-dimensional and classically demanding, while quantum algorithms face different bottlenecks: embedding nonlinear dynamics into a linear computation, loading dense field-interaction data, and efficiently extracting information. We present an end-to-end quantum algorithm, with rigorous convergence guarantees, for a weakly nonlinear kinetic plasma model. The system describes a 3D electron-ion plasma with adiabatic electrons, kinetic ions, Debye screening, and Krook relaxation. After Fourier-Hermite truncation, the dynamics reduces to a high-dimensional quadratic ordinary differential equation. To tackle quantum bottlenecks we combine three key ingredients. First, we use a plasma free energy to identify a Lyapunov transform under which a Carleman linear embedding converges exponentially in the truncation order within a certified weakly nonlinear regime. Second, we develop a hierarchical block-encoding protocol for dense matrices, exploiting the spatial decay of the field to avoid polynomial overhead from sparse access encodings. Third, we introduce a subroutine for information extraction that exploits nonlinear components encoded in the full Carleman history state to improve the estimation of linear observables. We construct a quantum algorithm to estimate the spacetime-averaged kinetic energy using $\widetilde{O}\!\left( N_F N_H^{1/2} \operatorname{polylog}\!\left(\frac{T}ε\right)\frac{1}ε\right)$ gates and $\widetilde{O}\!\left(\log\!\left(N_F N_H^{1/2}T\right)\log\!\left(\frac{1}ε\right)\right)$ qubits, where $N_F$ and $N_H$ are the Fourier and Hermite cutoffs. Relative to a Fourier-Hermite spectral solver, this yields exponential memory savings and superquadratic improvements in time. Together, these results establish a controlled nonlinear plasma benchmark for quantum simulation.
summary: This paper presents a novel end-to-end quantum algorithm designed to simulate weakly nonlinear plasma physics, which is classically demanding. It overcomes key quantum bottlenecks by employing advanced techniques like Lyapunov transforms and hierarchical block-encoding for dense matrices. The resulting algorithm promises exponential memory savings and superquadratic time speedups over existing classical spectral methods.
main_problem: Developing an end-to-end quantum algorithm capable of simulating weakly nonlinear plasma physics with a superquadratic speedup over classical methods.
main_result: The proposed quantum algorithm achieves rigorous convergence guarantees, yielding exponential memory savings and superquadratic time improvements relative to standard spectral solvers for the kinetic energy estimation.
method: The approach combines three novel ingredients: using a Lyapunov transform for an exponentially converging Carleman linear embedding, developing a hierarchical block-encoding protocol for dense matrices, and introducing a specialized subroutine for information extraction from the full history state.
model_or_system: The system is a 3D electron–ion plasma modeled by the Vlasov-Poisson system. The dynamics are simplified via Fourier–Hermite truncation to a high-dimensional quadratic ordinary differential equation, analyzed in a controlled perturbative regime.
key_observables: Spacetime-averaged kinetic energy moment ($\langle K angle$), and the nonlinearity strength ($\varphi_{\max}$).
important_parameters: Nonlinearity strength $\varphi(x, t)$, Fourier cutoff ($N_F$), Hermite cutoff ($N_H$), simulation time $T$, and error tolerance $\epsilon$.
main_assumptions: The analytical convergence guarantees are strictly limited to nonlinearities significantly weaker than those typically encountered in practice ($\varphi_{\max} \ll 1$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the convergence regimes based on nonlinearity strength ($\varphi_{\max}$), showing transitions between analytically certified Carleman-convergence and breakdown limits for different initial data types (Fourier vs. Gaussian).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model, addresses quantum bottlenecks (nonlinear embedding, dense encoding), presents the combined algorithmic framework with complexity analysis, and concludes by deriving bounds on key parameters like $\varphi_{\max}$ and estimating observables like $\langle K angle$.
why_interesting: While focused on plasma physics, the core technical contributions—developing block-encoding for nonlinear dynamics and achieving superquadratic speedups in quantum simulation of complex PDEs—are highly relevant to simulating general non-equilibrium many-body systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Narrowing down the convergence regime. Schematic illustration of convergence regimes for the weakly nonlinear Vlasov-Poisson model with collisions used to benchmark our quantum algorithm. As the nonlinearity strength φmax increases, the problem of simulating the plasma model defined by Eqs. (4–5) passes from an analytically certified Carleman-convergence regime, through a weakly nonlinear regime whose practical convergence threshold remains to be determined numerically or by alternative methods. Finally we pass to the limits of the model φmax = O(1), where the weakly nonlinear plasma model itself ceases to apply. The indicated values are computed for the Gaussian example in Fig. 3.

FIG. 2. Provably resolved plasma nonlinearities for plane-wave initial data. Shown in the above contour plot is nonlinearity measure φmax from Theorem 1 for which we can rigorously prove exponential convergence of the quan- tum algorithm. This places a simple analytic bound on the strength of nonlinearities that can be resolved. Further anal- ysis is needed to determine if stronger nonlinearities can also be simulated. We set n0 = (1, 0, 0), τ = 1, L = 103, and NH = ⌈NF/10⌉. The point (∆x, ¯ν) = (π, 10−2), on which φmax = 7.12 × 10−8, is indicated by the ×.

FIG. 3. Provably resolved plasma nonlinearities for Gaussian initial data. Shown in the above contour plot is nonlinearity measure φmax corresponding to the Gaussian initial data (13) for which we can rigorously prove exponential convergence of the quantum algorithm. We set σ = 10, τ = 1, L = 103, and NH = ⌈NF/10⌉. The point (∆x, ¯ν) = (π, 10−2), on which φmax = 2.08 × 10−5, is indicated by the ×. See Section II C 5 for details.

FIG. 4. Hierarchical decomposition of a 2-d kernel: The combinatorics of the hierarchical decomposition for a 2-d kernel, with N = 16, ℓmax = log2 16 = 4. The red square is the reference, and the selected 2-clusters, 3-clusters and 4-clusters have been highlighted. Can be extended to 3 dimensions in a straightforward manner.
